title: The Son shares the Father’s greatness
source_text: Πλήν φησιν ὁ Κέλσος ἡμᾶς ἀποκρίνεσθαι εἰκότι στοχασμῷ, ὁμολογῶν ἀναγράφειν ἡμῶν τὴν ἀπόκρισιν οὕτως ἔχουσαν· ἐπειδὴ μέγας ἐστὶ καὶ δυσθεώρητος ὁ θεὸς, πνεῦμα ἴδιον ἐμβαλὼν εἰς σῶμα ἡμῖν ὅμοιον δεῦρο κατέπεμψεν, ὡς ἂν δυνηθείημεν ἀκοῦσαι παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ μαθεῖν. οὐ μόνος δὲ μέγας καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐστιν ὁ τῶν ὅλων θεὸς καὶ πατήρ· μετέδωκε γὰρ ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τῆς μεγαλειότητος τῷ μονογενεῖ καὶ πρωτοτόκῳ „πάσης κτίσεως“· ἵν᾿ „εἰκὼν“ αὐτὸς τυγχάνων „τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ“ καὶ ἐν τῷ μεγέθει σῴζῃ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ πατρός. οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν εἶναι σύμμετρον, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, καὶ καλὴν εἰκόνα „τοῦ ἀοράτου θεοῦ,“ μὴ καὶ τοῦ μεγέθους παριστᾶσαν τὴν εἰκόνα. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ θεὸς καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς τῷ μὲν μὴ εἶναι σῶμα ἀόρατός ἐστιν· τοῖς δὲ θεωρητικοῖς καρδίᾳ θεωρητὸς, τουτέστι νῷ, καρδίᾳ δὲ οὐ τῇ τυχούσῃ ἀλλὰ τῇ καθαρᾷ. οὐ γὰρ θέμις μεμολυσμένην καρδίαν ἐνορᾶν θεῷ, ἀλλὰ δεῖ καθαρὸν εἶναι τὸ τοῦ καθαροῦ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν θεωρητικόν. ἔστω δὴ καὶ δυσθεώρητος ὁ θεός· ἀλλ᾿ οὐ μόνος δυσθεώρητός ἐστι τινὶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ μονογενὴς αὐτοῦ. δυσθεώρητος γὰρ ὁ θεὸς λόγος, δυσθεώρητος δὲ οὑτωσὶ καὶ σοφία ἐστὶν, ἐν ᾗ τὰ πάντα πεποίηκεν ὁ θεός. τίς γὰρ δύναται καθ᾿ ἕκαστον τῶν πάντων τὴν σοφίαν, ἐν ᾗ ὁ θεὸς καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν πάντων πεποίηκε, (θεωρῆσαι) ; οὐ διὰ τὸ δυσθεώρητος οὖν ὁ θεὸς εἶναι ὡς εὐθεώρητον τὸν υἱὸν ἔπεμψεν. ἅπερ μὴ νοήσας ὁ Κέλσος εἶπεν ὡς ἐκ προσώπου ἡμῶν· διὰ τὸ δυσθεώρητος εἶναι πνεῦμα ἴδιον ἐμβαλὼν εἰς σῶμα ἡμῖν ὅμοιον δεῦρο κατέπεμψεν, ὡς ἂν δυνηθείημεν ἀκοῦσαί τε παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ μαθεῖν. ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ἀποδεδώκαμεν, καὶ ὁ υἱὸς δυσθεώρητος ὢν, ἅτε λόγος θεὸς, δι᾿ οὗ τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο, „καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν.“
pass_a_gloss: Yet (πλήν) Celsus says that we answer by a likely conjecture (εἰκὼς στοχασμός), agreeing/acknowledging (ὁμολογῶν) that he writes down (ἀναγράφω) our answer being thus: since God is great (μέγας) and hard to behold (δυσθεώρητος), having put (ἐμβάλλω) his own spirit (πνεῦμα ἴδιον) into a body like (ὅμοιος) to us he sent (it) down (καταπέμπω) here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn (μανθάνω). Not alone great according to us (καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς) is the God and Father of the whole (ὁ τῶν ὅλων θεὸς καὶ πατήρ); for he gave a share (μεταδίδωμι) of himself and of his greatness (μεγαλειότης) to the only-begotten (μονογενής) and firstborn (πρωτότοκος) 'of all creation (κτίσις)', in order that he, being 'image (εἰκών) of the invisible (ἀόρατος) God', might preserve (σῴζω) also in magnitude (μέγεθος) the image of the Father. For it was not possible to be a symmetrical/well-proportioned (σύμμετρος), so I may name it, and beautiful (καλός) image 'of the invisible God' not also presenting (παρίστημι) the image of the greatness. But also God according to us by not being body (σῶμα) is invisible; but to the contemplative (θεωρητικός) is beholdable (θεωρητός) by heart (καρδία), that is mind (νοῦς), heart not any chance one but the pure (καθαρός). For it is not lawful (θέμις) for a defiled (μολύνω) heart to look upon (ἐνοράω) God, but what is worthily (κατ᾿ ἀξίαν) contemplative of the pure must be pure. Let God then be hard to behold; but he is not alone hard to behold to anyone (τινί), but also his only-begotten. For hard to behold is God the Word, and hard to behold in this way also is Wisdom (σοφία), in which God has made (ποιέω) all things. For who is able in respect of each of all things to behold the wisdom in which God made each of all things? Not then on account of God's being hard to behold did he send the Son as easy to behold (εὐθεώρητος). Not having understood (νοέω) which, Celsus spoke as from our person (ἐκ προσώπου ἡμῶν): on account of being hard to behold, having put his own spirit into a body like to us he sent (it) down here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn. But as we have rendered (ἀποδίδωμι), also the Son being hard to behold, as God the Word, through whom all things came to be (γίνομαι), 'also tabernacled (σκηνόω) in/among us'.

lemmas.lemma: ὁ τῶν ὅλων θεὸς καὶ πατήρ

pass_b_english: Celsus, however, says that we answer with a likely guess, and he acknowledges that he is writing down our answer in this form: “Since God is great and hard to behold, he put his own spirit into a body like ours and sent it down here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn.”

But in our teaching the God and Father of all is not the only one who is great. For he has given a share of himself and of his greatness to the only-begotten and “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), so that, being himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), he might keep the image of the Father in greatness too. For there could not have been a well-proportioned image, if I may call it that, and a beautiful image “of the invisible God,” that did not also present the image of his greatness.

Further, in our teaching God is invisible because he is not a body; but to those who can contemplate him he can be beheld with the heart, that is, with the mind; and not with just any heart, but with a pure one (Matthew 5:8). For it is not right for a defiled heart to gaze on God; what would behold the Pure One as he deserves must itself be pure.

Granted, then, that God is hard to behold; yet he is not the only one hard to behold, but so is his only-begotten. For God the Word is hard to behold, and in the same way so is the Wisdom in which God made all things (Psalm 104:24). For who can behold, in each and every thing, the Wisdom in which God made each and every thing? It was not, then, because God is hard to behold that he sent the Son as one easy to behold.

Celsus did not understand this, and said, as though speaking for us: “Because he is hard to behold, he put his own spirit into a body like ours and sent it down here, so that we might be able to hear from him and learn.” But, as we have explained, the Son too, though he is hard to behold, since he is God the Word through whom all things came to be (John 1:3), also “dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

choices.choice: Celsus’s words (given twice, the second time slightly shorter, beginning ‘because he is hard to behold’) are in double quotation marks. εἰκότι στοχασμῷ (‘with a likely guess’) may be Celsus’s own phrase, but Origen reports it indirectly, so it is not quoted. ὁμολογῶν ἀναγράφειν is unclear: rendered ‘he acknowledges that he is writing down our answer’, i.e. Celsus admits he is putting the answer in our mouths. πνεῦμα in Celsus’s mouth is kept lowercase ‘spirit’, since he uses the word in a physical, Stoic sense (see 6.71). Colossians 1:15 is quoted twice (‘firstborn of all creation’; ‘image of the invisible God’); τῷ μονογενεῖ καὶ πρωτοτόκῳ keeps both titles joined by ‘and’. The pure heart that sees God is a clear allusion to Matthew 5:8. ‘Wisdom in which God made all things’ alludes to Psalm 104:24 (LXX 103:24, πάντα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐποίησας), converted to English numbering; Wisdom is capitalised both times, since Origen means the Son. τοῦ καθαροῦ is taken as masculine, ‘the Pure One’ (God); neuter ‘what is pure’ is possible. τινί after δυσθεώρητος (‘hard for anyone to behold’) is absorbed into ‘hard to behold’. Koetschau supplies (θεωρῆσαι); followed. The last sentence is elliptical in the Greek (καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ... καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν); rendered as one clause with ‘also dwelt among us’.
'to the only-begotten, the "firstborn of all creation"' to 'to the only-begotten and "firstborn of all creation"' (τῷ μονογενεῖ καὶ πρωτοτόκῳ: two titles joined by καί)
'he could not have been a well-proportioned image ... without' to 'there could not have been a well-proportioned image ... that did not' (οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν εἶναι: impersonal)
'and so also, in the same way, is the Wisdom' to 'and in the same way so is the Wisdom' (doubled phrase)
'in each one of all things ... each one of all things' to 'in each and every thing' (calque)
second 'wisdom' capitalised to match the first: same referent, the Son
